Following suggestions for my post here "Should results of a journal paper always be reproducible?", I have done the simulation using a particular seed in the first part of my result section. Now the issues are, how to mention that particular seed in the paper. 4 follow a fixed topology generated by pseudo-random. seed (1010) to validate the scheme. ## 2 Answers 2. A seed for a pseudo-random number generator is a sufficiently well-known concept in numerical simulations that the seed, on its own, probably does not require a citation—you can simply state which seed you used. The pseudo-random number generator algorithm, however, may need to be cited, particularly if it's not a well-known algorithm. If you are aiming for your results to be completely reproducible, you will need the random-generator seed, however you will also need the source code (unless you use only one predefined method in a very clear way) and sometimes even other information such as the version of employed software, operating system, and hardware specs. The random seed is of no use to the reader on its own, and hence there is no point in mentioning it here. That you control this with seeds (instead of say saving and loading them) is a technical detail that should have no relevance to your results. I would put the seeds together with the source code and other relevant details in a supplement (or similar). At most I would mention the specific seed when referencing this supplement in a way that makes clear to the reader that this information only makes sense together with the supplement:. The results in Fig. 2, 3, and 4 were obtained for the same realisation of the topology (Supplement A, seed 1010) to validate the scheme. ## You must log in to answer this question. Find centralized, trusted content and collaborate around the technologies you use most. # Reproducible results with parallel\_for and random numbers possible? I have code which involves some heavy computations so I use the parallel\_for loop in Visual Studio C++. This works fine and the code runs much faster in comparison with a normal for loop. My problem is that I want reproducible results but the computations involve random numbers. I can use a fixed seed but this does seem to work when using a parallel\_for loop. std::uniform_real_distribution<double> d(-1.0, 1.0);. static std::mt19937 mt(seed);. for (volatile int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i). for (size_t i = 0; i < 10; ++i) { expensive_function(); }. for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) test();. When I use a normal for loop instead of parallel\_for (`USE_PAR = 0`), I reproducibly get the same output every time I run the program:. But with the parallel\_for loop (`USE_PAR = 1`), I get a different result everytime. For example the first time:. And then the second time:. Is it possible to have both? Good performance with parallel\_for and reproducible results even if random numbers are used? ## 1 Answer 1. The reason is because you have undefined behavior. `thread_local std::mt19937 mt(seed);`. Note: I don't know the `<ppl.h>` library, but making a variable `volatile` is pointless as long as the variable is under the program's control (that is, not connected to some external hardware that may change it). Drop the `volatile int i` and make it `int i`. Thanks for contributing an answer to Stack Overflow! results.content:
Title: Random seeds and reproducible results in PyTorch | by Vandana Rajan | Medium
# Random seeds and reproducible results in PyTorch. Many a time, while building and evaluating neural network based models in PyTorch, I found that the results can be sensitive to the seed values used. In this article, I will talk about random seeds and their effects and how to obtain reproducible results in PyTorch. This is the expected behavior since we are asking the system to give us ‘random’ numbers and not deterministic numbers and the state of the random number generator (RNG) changes with every call to the function. >>> import torch>>> random_seed = 1>>> torch.manual_seed(random_seed)<torch._C.Generator object at 0x7ff97e751890>>>> torch.rand(1,3)tensor()>>> torch.manual_seed(random_seed)<torch._C.Generator object at 0x7ff97e751890>>>> torch.rand(1,3)tensor(). This is because we set the seed to the same value in between both the function calls. Also, we have the function ‘torch.set\_rng\_state()’ to set the RNG to a per-determined state (can be a state obtained using ‘torch.get\_rng\_state()). >>> import torch>>> w = torch.empty(3,5) # an empty weight matrix>>> torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(w)tensor([[ 0.2818,  0.5715,  0.4295,  0.3528, -0.1703],        [-0.6360, -0.5974,  0.0125, -0.3813,  0.6985],        [-0.1623,  0.1439,  0.5289,  0.4810,  0.1967]])>>> torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(w)tensor([[ 0.5661, -0.2702, -1.1051,  1.0565, -0.0020],        [ 0.6900, -0.6753,  0.1727,  0.2523,  0.9107],        [-0.0907, -0.4757,  0.2029, -0.7582,  0.3661]])>>> torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(w)tensor([[ 1.1410, -0.6040,  0.5560,  1.1087, -0.2134],        [ 0.5073, -0.0910,  0.3091,  0.0196,  0.4631],        [-0.4798,  0.1759, -0.2020,  0.8792, -0.2073]])>>> random_seed = 1>>> torch.manual_seed(random_seed)<torch._C.Generator object at 0x7ff97e751890>>>> torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(w)tensor([[ 0.3307,  0.1335,  0.0308,  0.3107, -0.2260],        [-0.0831, -0.7614,  0.1908, -0.5138, -0.2815],        [-0.4461, -0.0291, -0.0978, -0.4828,  0.2112]])>>> torch.manual_seed(random_seed)<torch._C.Generator object at 0x7ff97e751890>>>> torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(w)tensor([[ 0.3307,  0.1335,  0.0308,  0.3107, -0.2260],        [-0.0831, -0.7614,  0.1908, -0.5138, -0.2815],        [-0.4461, -0.0291, -0.0978, -0.4828,  0.2112]]). Here, we can see that the **initial weight values obtained depends on the state of the RNG,** which is why when I set the seed before every call to the init function, I can get the same initial weight values. Now that we have seen the effects of seed and the state of random number generator, we can look at how to obtain reproducible results in PyTorch. >>> import torch>>> random_seed = 1 # or any of your favorite number >>> torch.manual_seed(random_seed)>>> torch.cuda.manual_seed(random_seed)>>> torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True>>> torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False>>> import numpy as np>>> np.random.seed(random_seed).
